US inflation is diverging from the Fed’s target:

US CPI Inflation has surged +30.2% since January 2020, to an all-time high.

This translates into an annualized inflation rate of +4.0% over this period.

Meanwhile, under a steady 2% annual inflation target, cumulative CPI growth would have been just +14.3%.

In other words, actual cumulative inflation is +15.9 percentage points above the target path, more than double the implied increase.

This comes as CPI has remained above 2% for 67 consecutive months.

The gap began widening again in March, as inflation has now remained above 3% for 7 consecutive months.

Asset owners are the only winners.

On the Nvidia situation:

Nvidia's board can still make things right.

It has now been 48 hours since Jensen Huang resigned from his role as CEO, President, and board member of Nvidia.

Meanwhile, a thorough investigation has not been completed, countless critical questions are unanswered, and one of the world's greatest CEOs was forced out before the full facts of the situation were established.

In fact, the US Attorney General, the CIA, the DNI, and members of the House Intelligence Committee have also suggested that the current evidence remains inconclusive regarding whether Jensen Huang was involved in an affair with a Chinese spy.

The reality is that Jensen Huang resigned in the heat of the moment and the board acted based on speculative information.

We believe Nvidia's board, $NVDA, has a duty to shareholders to openly acknowledge that Jensen Huang could return to the company, pending a thorough investigation.

What happens in a CEO's personal life should not automatically dictate his role in a company, particularly if an investigation fails to establish national security misconduct or other wrongdoing that warrants removal.

The right move is to acknowledge that Jensen Huang is innocent until proven guilty.

Nvidia's board must do this now. It is not too late.

BREAKING: China’s trade surplus surged +$84 billion YoY in the first 10 months of 2026, or +8.8%, to a record $1.04 trillion.

This marks the 3rd consecutive YoY increase for this period of the year, totalling +$348 billion.

China’s 2026 surplus has already surpassed every previous full-year total except 2025, when it rose to a record $1.18 trillion.

In October alone, the trade surplus increased +$17 billion YoY, to $105 billion.

This comes as exports jumped +35% YoY, to $412 billion, their 3rd-highest on record, while imports surged +42% YoY, to $307 billion, their 2nd-highest on record.

China's dominance in international trade is accelerating amid the AI investment wave.

US credit stress is intensifying among the weakest-quality borrowers:

Spreads on CCC-rated and lower US corporate bonds are up to 13.3%, near the highest since the 2020 pandemic.

Since January 2026, this figure has surged +490 basis points.

As a result, these spreads have now surpassed the 2022 bear market peak of 12.9%.

For perspective, during the 2020 February-March surge, this metric peaked at 18.8%.

Meanwhile, the spread differential between CCC- and BBB-rated corporate debt has widened to ~1,200 basis points, its widest level in at least 5 years.

This means investors are demanding ~12 percentage points more in compensation to hold the lowest-rated debt rather than first-notch investment-grade corporate bonds.

Cracks are spreading quickly through the lowest-quality credit.

US layoffs continue to slow sharply:

US job cut announcements dropped -71% YoY in October, to 43,994, the lowest October total since 2023.

Year-to-date announcements have declined -44% YoY, to 617,189, the lowest January-October total since 2022.

This is also the 8th month of 2026 with job cuts down YoY versus the corresponding month of the prior year.

Food companies led October layoffs with 9,677 cuts, while Technology has recorded the most reductions year-to-date, at 171,501, up +21% YoY.

Market and economic conditions accounted for 16,407 announced job cuts in October, or ~37% of all layoffs, bringing the year-to-date total to 130,531, overtaking AI as the most cited reason.

US employers appear to be slowing job cuts.
